overview:
Adana-nikshepana-samiti (Sanskrit: ādāna-nikṣepaṇa-samiti, often shortened to ādāna-nikṣepa-samiti) is one of the classical five forms of samiti, or carefulness, in Jain ethics. Samiti refers to deliberate, mindful regulation of bodily, verbal, and mental activity so that violence (hiṃsā), carelessness (pramāda), and attachment (rāga) are minimized. Within this framework, adana-nikshepana-samiti specifically governs the acts of taking up (ādāna) and putting down (nikṣepaṇa) objects—such as utensils, scriptures, tools, clothing, or any item that may affect living beings in its vicinity.

In both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions, adana-nikshepana-samiti is taught as a practical discipline that trains the practitioner to be aware of the spatial and ecological consequences of their movements. When one lifts an object, the ground beneath it may contain minute organisms; when one sets it down, the new surface may also host subtle forms of life. Jain thought holds that careless handling of objects can crush, displace, or otherwise harm these beings. Thus, adana-nikshepana-samiti requires slow, attentive, and non-impulsive movement, often accompanied by visual inspection of the area, gentle placement, and avoidance of unnecessary shifting.

For mendicants, this samiti is codified in monastic codes (cāritra) and daily conduct rules, shaping how they handle alms bowls, brooms, scriptures, and seating arrangements. The discipline is not merely external; it is tied to inner attitudes of reverence for life and non-possession (aparigraha). A monk or nun is expected to avoid ostentatious or restless handling of objects, and to treat even simple tools as instruments that must not become causes of harm. Lay followers (śrāvakas and śrāvikās) are also encouraged to adopt a moderated form of adana-nikshepana-samiti in domestic life—for example, in how they move furniture, store food, or clean floors—though the intensity and ritualization differ from mendicant practice.

Philosophically, adana-nikshepana-samiti is linked to the broader Jain doctrine of karma and the gradations of violence. Even unintentional harm can bind karmic particles to the soul (jīva), especially when accompanied by negligence or indifference. By cultivating carefulness in taking and placing objects, the practitioner reduces the scope of inadvertent injury and thereby lessens the influx (āsrava) of karmic matter. Commentarial literature often emphasizes that samiti does not guarantee absolute non-violence—since subtle life forms are pervasive—but it significantly refines the practitioner’s sensitivity and responsibility.

In the canonical and post-canonical texts, adana-nikshepana-samiti is frequently mentioned together with the other four samitis: iryā-samiti (carefulness in walking), bhāṣā-samiti (carefulness in speech), eṣaṇā-samiti (carefulness in seeking alms or resources), and utsarga-samiti (carefulness in disposal or excretion). Together, these five form a core ethical technology for regulating everyday conduct. Adana-nikshepana-samiti occupies a middle position in this list, bridging movement (iryā) and resource-seeking (eṣaṇā) with the concrete handling of objects. Its role in Jain practice is therefore both symbolic—embodying respect for all life—and highly practical, shaping the micro-gestures of daily living.

Modern expositions of Jain ethics often highlight adana-nikshepana-samiti as an example of ecological mindfulness and embodied non-violence. While contemporary practitioners may not follow all monastic prescriptions, the underlying principle remains relevant: to be aware of how one’s physical interactions with the environment can cause harm, and to cultivate habits that minimize such impact. In this sense, adana-nikshepana-samiti can be seen as an early articulation of what today might be called "ethical ergonomics" or "non-violent handling"—a disciplined way of moving through the world that honors the pervasive presence of life.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi (traditionally attributed)
primary_sources.translation: Carefulness in walking, speech, taking and placing, and disposal are the samitis.
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārthasūtra 7.5 (chapter on conduct) lists the five samitis as fundamental forms of carefulness. The sūtra itself is terse; later commentaries such as Pūjyapāda’s Sarvārthasiddhi elaborate that ādāna-nikṣepa-samiti concerns the mindful taking up and putting down of objects so as to avoid harm to living beings. The text is accepted as authoritative in both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions, though there are minor variations in wording across editions.

primary_sources.title: Sarvārthasiddhi (Commentary on Tattvārthasūtra)
primary_sources.author: Pūjyapāda Devanandi (Digambara)
primary_sources.original_text: आदानं नामोपकरणादीनां गृहीतिः, निक्षेपो नाम तेषां यथास्थानं विनिवेशः। तत्र यथासंभवमवधानेन क्रियमाणमादान-निक्षेपणं समितिर्भवति।
primary_sources.transliteration: ādānaṃ nāmopakaraṇādīnāṃ gṛhītiḥ, nikṣepo nāma teṣāṃ yathāsthānaṃ viniveśaḥ. tatra yathāsaṃbhavam avadhānena kriyamāṇam ādāna-nikṣepaṇaṃ samitir bhavati.
primary_sources.translation: Taking (ādāna) is the grasping of implements and the like; placing (nikṣepa) is the setting of them down in their proper location. When such taking and placing are performed, as far as possible, with attentiveness, they become samiti.
primary_sources.notes: This passage explains the technical meaning of adana-nikshepana-samiti in the Digambara tradition. It clarifies that the same physical actions—grasping and setting down—are ethically transformed into samiti when done with awareness and concern for non-violence. The commentary also links this carefulness to the reduction of inadvertent harm to subtle life forms.

primary_sources.title: Ratnakaraṇḍa-śrāvakācāra
primary_sources.author: Samantabhadra (Digambara, traditional attribution)
primary_sources.translation: The five samitis are carefulness in walking, speech, seeking (alms or resources), taking and placing, and disposal.
primary_sources.notes: Ratnakaraṇḍa-śrāvakācāra is a key Digambara manual for lay conduct. By listing adana-nikshepana-samiti among the five samitis, it extends the relevance of this discipline beyond monastic life. Later verses and commentaries encourage lay followers to adopt moderated forms of these carefulness practices in household activities.

primary_sources.title: Śvetāmbara monastic codes (e.g., Chedasūtras)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous canonical redactors (Śvetāmbara)
primary_sources.original_text: While specific phrasing varies, passages in texts such as the Vyavahāra and Niśītha Chedasūtras regulate how monks and nuns should take up and set down bowls, brooms, and other requisites, emphasizing inspection of the ground and gentle placement.
primary_sources.transliteration: N/A (multiple Prakrit passages across different sections)
primary_sources.translation: Representative instructions: "One should lift and place the bowl after examining the ground, avoiding harm to living beings."
primary_sources.notes: Śvetāmbara Chedasūtra literature operationalizes adana-nikshepana-samiti through detailed rules on handling monastic requisites. Although the term samiti may not always be explicitly used in each rule, the underlying concept of careful taking and placing is central. These texts show how the abstract category of samiti is translated into concrete disciplinary regulations.

misconceptions.myth: Adana-nikshepana-samiti is only about ritualized movements of monks and has no relevance for laypeople.
misconceptions.reality: While the most detailed prescriptions for adana-nikshepana-samiti appear in monastic codes, Jain lay manuals and modern teachers explicitly encourage householders to adopt its spirit in daily life—such as careful handling of furniture, utensils, and cleaning tools—to reduce harm to living beings. The intensity and form differ, but the principle of mindful taking and placing is shared.

misconceptions.myth: Adana-nikshepana-samiti is merely a matter of etiquette or aesthetic grace in movement.
misconceptions.reality: Jain texts ground adana-nikshepana-samiti in the doctrine of non-violence and karma, not in social etiquette. The carefulness is ethically motivated: it aims to minimize injury to subtle life forms and reduce karmic influx. Graceful movement may result, but it is a by-product of ethical discipline rather than the primary goal.

misconceptions.myth: If one practices adana-nikshepana-samiti perfectly, no violence at all occurs.
misconceptions.reality: Classical Jain authors acknowledge that in a world permeated by subtle life forms, some level of inadvertent harm is nearly unavoidable. Samiti, including adana-nikshepana-samiti, does not guarantee absolute non-violence; instead, it significantly reduces harm and refines the practitioner’s sensitivity and responsibility. The aim is minimization of hiṃsā and pramāda, not metaphysical perfection in ordinary activity.

misconceptions.myth: Adana-nikshepana-samiti is a minor, optional practice that can be ignored without affecting one’s ethical progress.
misconceptions.reality: In major doctrinal texts like Tattvārthasūtra, the five samitis—including adana-nikshepana-samiti—are presented as foundational elements of right conduct. Commentaries link them to the regulation of everyday behavior and the reduction of karmic bondage. While individual capacity and context may vary, traditional Jain ethics treats samiti as integral to serious spiritual practice, not as an optional refinement.
